utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, you have some more questions? Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Good morning, Excellencies, good morning to everyone. [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Skoko. [In English] I will not do anything in examination-in-chief right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then yes, good morning, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Skoko, I see that you have a number of papers in front of you. Could you please, apart from your statement, put the documents to one side before I start asking you some questions. Thank you. You joined the SDS in 1990; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I joined the SDS, as far as I can remember, sometime in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall in one of the Assembly sessions, in fact, at the 33rd Session in July 1993 that you stated in that Assembly session that you had been a member of the party for three years?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any statements from that Assembly -- well, that is said in tentative terms. It's hard to say. I don't know which month that was. I don't really think it matters that much, does it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. You said that you joined in 1991, sometime in 1991. You remained a member throughout the conflict in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Are you still a member now?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not an active member of the party.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In your statement you said that you were the director of the Republika Srpska electricity supply board from August 1992 to February 1993, at which time you left the post. And you said that after you left the post you continued to work as an advisor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you left the post in February 1993 you didn't work for some time, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did work as an advisor at the electricity company, as I've already said. Also as I said in my statement, I worked on scientific research in terms of analysis and providing opinions about different peace plans that were topical at the time in terms of resolving the conflict in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did you mean then when you said at the -- again at the 33rd Session in July 1993 at the Assembly session that you haven't been working for four months now, what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time, in fact, in February 1993 I was dismissed by a lobby, a group of interests in Republika Srpska. As you know during every conflict there are interest groups and lobbies, so in fact I was involved in a dispute in order to return to my previous position because I thought that was done against the law, against the constitution, so that was my remark to the Assembly --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. -- Dr. Skoko, if I can --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were about to say that was your remark to the Assembly. What I wanted to know was what were you doing between February and July?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came to work to the electricity company. Basically I played the role of advisor. I came to the electricity company as I would, I received my salary. I worked on the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did you -- what were you advising on specifically? You said you worked on and then the interpreter didn't catch the last part of your sentence.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you know, at the time the electricity board, or rather, the electricity in Republika Srpska as such was totally destroyed, so I was supposed to provide advice on enhancing energy facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And who did you advise specifically? Who did you provide this advice to?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The director-general at the time was Mr. Nikola Erceg. Mr. Drago Skulic [phoen] was the technical director so I co-operated with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said in your statement that there were four incomplete municipalities within the federal Sarajevo, and that's Stari Grad, Novi Grad, Novo Sarajevo and Centar. In fact, during the conflict there were six municipalities in whole or in part inside the front lines of Bosnian-held territory in Sarajevo. Before you mentioned plus Ilidza and Vogosca; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I did not quite understand that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said in your statement that there were four municipalities within the federal Sarajevo. You in fact said four incomplete municipalities. You said Stari Grad, Novi Grad, Novo Sarajevo, and Centar, but in fact there's two additional municipalities, that is, Ilidza and Vogosca which were also -- had part of their territory within the front -- inside the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the municipality of Stari Grad, the old city, was also the Serb municipality. However, the part that you mention was a marginal part, that is to say a marginal part in the following sense: The number of households that were supposed to be provided with electricity. That was a very marginal number.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that the number of households in Sarajevo may have been approximately 40.000 for the four municipalities you mentioned. You don't have a source for that in your statement. That's -- do you? That's just your estimate?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, in accordance with the 1991 census, these four urban municipalities that I spoke of had a population of 195.000 Muslims. That's the census of 1991. If you take into account that the largest number of Serbs from those four municipalities had already left, or rather, a marginal number stayed on during the war, that's it. Some Muslims came in the meantime so that would be 200 to 250.000 inhabitants. If we take into account the fact that an average Muslim family had five or six members of household then that would be from 35 to 40.000 households on average.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Are you aware of the Sarajevo household survey conducted in 1994 by an NGO called the Institute for the Research of Crimes against Humanity in International Law Sarajevo which interviewed and received results from 85.000 different households within the front lines of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that information, but please. As I worked on this material that I have been speaking about, I worked at the republican institute for social planning which was the central planning institution for all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So when I'm presenting this information I am presenting official information, official data of the republican institute for statistics of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, and Mr. Karadzic, the reference to the household survey can be found at Exhibit P04997 which is e-court page 1, footnote 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Skoko, you say that it follows that if you take all of the electricity -- if you take that all of the electricity was used for households, the average monthly consumption was 308 kilowatt hours per household. Assuming your figures are correct regarding the amount of electricity that was available, you're overestimating the amount of electricity available to each household for at least two reasons and the first is that the figure of 308 kilowatt hours is based on all the electricity being used for households, yes?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, when I made these balances, I worked on all the electricity spent by households and that came through Serb-held territory plus 40 million kilowatt hours that the Muslim side had from their own sources. So that is a total of 590. If we divide it by four years, or rather, 46 months and 40.000 households, then the ultimate figure would be 308 kilowatt hours per household. So I was not taking into account consumption of schools, and so on and so forth. I cannot do all of that. I'm not saying that each and every household could receive 308 kilowatt hours because this electricity was largely used for the manufacturing of ammunition within Sarajevo and for various other purposes. Now, this quantity of electricity, did they distribute it that way? Did they check whether this energy was being used rationally or irrationally? I cannot go into that. I'm just saying how much electric and energy was available per household.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What you do, though, is you take the figure and then you divide it by 40.000 households and you come up with a figure of 308 kilowatt hours. But in fact, as we've just seen, the -- a survey in 1984 says there's 85.000 households in Sarajevo. That's number one. Number two, you would agree that hospitals were also using this electricity that was supplied to the city of Sarajevo, yes?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. It is possible that some households used electricity for heating as well. I cannot go into the internal distribution of electricity in terms of individual users.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. -- Dr. Skoko, not only hospitals, government buildings, UNPROFOR, humanitarian agencies, water pumping stationing, they all used the electricity that was coming into Sarajevo, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim that. I don't know that. Why would somebody use electricity for heating if there were large coal mines in the immediate vicinity of Sarajevo? So there are many cases that households used electricity for heating, but that was their own affair, how they would distribute that energy. I don't know that. How could I know who used electric energy and how? Please, this information about 80.000, that is simply impossible, it is simply impossible because I have used official data of the republican institute of statistics of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm saying that according to the 1991 census in the territory of these four municipalities that were under the control of the Muslims not to take into account the periphery of these municipalities that the Prosecutor spoke of, there was about 200 -- there was a population of about 200.000 Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Skoko, you were aware, are you not, of the interruption of all electricity supply from the 7th of December, 1992, through to the 15th of January, 1993, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak of any exact dates, but I know that from 1992 until almost the end of January 1993 there was shelling of the transformer station in Blazuj. On that occasion two transformers were totally destroyed, one of them leaked, so almost all of Sarajevo was left without any electricity including the Serb part of Sarajevo except for some of the marginal parts that were under Serb control.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you're also aware of Sarajevo being without electricity for 140 days in 1993, including 53 consecutive days?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that information that for 140 days Sarajevo was out -- was without any electric energy. I don't know where you get that information from.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter number 24909, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Skoko, this is a 1993 annual report from BH Elektroprivreda. If we could go to page 10 of the report. And if you can look at the fourth full paragraph starting: "The supply of Sarajevo by electricity was provided ..." And then the last sentence of that paragraph: "During 1993 the city was without electricity supply about 140 days. The longest ... period occurred from June 21st to August 13th (53 days)." Do you recall that occurring?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, first of all, this is a report of the Elektroprivreda of the Federation, that is to say the Muslim part. We don't have that report. I cannot give any comment with regard to these data. This is not a valid report that I could confirm. That is one thing. Secondly, I said a moment ago --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But do you recall -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not count the days during 1993, but 140 days that is impossible. A moment ago I said that the longest shortage was in January, the end of December 1992 and then January 1993. So according to our information that was approximately 45 days at the time. I think that this information is manipulated. 140 days, 53 days without any interruption, no I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this page of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. President, I think this page can be admitted for the context even though it's not confirmed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Probably the witness's microphone should be turned on again. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6269, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] The cover page and page 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Skoko, you said in your statement that there was radio contact between the TS in RS and the FBH for the purposes of the work of the EES. And you said that there was certain internal telephone lines between Sarajevo 10 which is the Reljevo station and the dispatches of the Sarajevo PCU plant situated in the building of the BH electricity supply board. Who were you in radio contact with on the Bosnian side?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally was not there. I attended meetings at Sarajevo airport a few times only. I was not involved in these contacts and it wasn't my duty to do that either. It was appropriate people who worked at transformer stations and maintained these contacts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned that there were disruptions on the transmission line from Visegrad to Sarajevo and you said that the Pretis weapons factory in Vogosca was prevented from operating. Did you know that the Bosnian Serbs connected a transmission line Poline-Pale in order to get an electricity line from Visegrad to Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And did you know that a power transformer was installed at the Pretis factory by September 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not aware of these details. That was not my task. This is purely operative work that persons involved in transformer maintenance are aware of. I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Karadzic, that's Exhibit D02545.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Going back to the previous document we just admitted, it was published in both languages at the time; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's my understanding, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it usual for this institution to produce an annual report in English and in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That I can't -- that I can't say, although I note that the 1992 annual report is also in both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Skoko, you said that -- well, it's your evidence that there was no interruption of the power supply to Sarajevo during the war except in the cases when the transmission lines were damaged. This leaves open the possibility for damaged transmission lines to stay damaged for long periods of time due to, for example, denial of access for repairs, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure what your question is. There were interruptions, but please the electric system is very complex. It can function only when production, transmission, distribution, consumption, and system management are fully harmonised. If any of these segments at any point in time doesn't work well, the system falls, it crashes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Skoko, it's true, isn't it, that during the conflict Bosnian Serb authorities denied access to locations where repairs were to be carried out?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The repairs weren't only carried out by the Bosnian authorities. There were joint teams formed by UNPROFOR and they went to the ground. Most times the interruptions were at the demarcation line. I don't know to what extent the Bosnian authorities in Sarajevo were active or what they did and why there were interruptions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So you're not aware of the Bosnian Serbs denying access to any repair locations?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with such reports about the obstruction of the Bosnian Serbs when it comes to repairs. I'm not saying that there hasn't been any obstruction from either side, but I don't mean systemic obstruction. But during the war it would happen that a soldier would shoot at a transformer in order to fill a container with oil that he would use as fuel, but systemic obstruction was not present in the sense that somebody ordered obstruction. I'm not saying that there weren't individual incidents like as drunken soldiers shooting at a transformer station or something of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter number 24262, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Skoko, this is a monthly UNPROFOR report for July 1993, and if we can see at the bottom of page 1 under the heading 1.1 Electricity, it says: "Electricity is and will remain the key of all the utilities problems inside the sector. All the others are connected with. Serbs denied any access to the repair location on the line which is supplying the town (Reljevo/Vogosca)." This shows the Serbs were obstructing electricity supply which is contrary to your unequivocal statement that nobody from Republika Srpska ever obstructed the power supply to Sarajevo, isn't it -- doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Serbs. I don't know what is meant by that. Maybe it refers to a group of soldiers or a group of citizens, but I'm saying that nobody from the official authorities of the Republika Srpska starting from President Karadzic down to me, the director of Elektroprivreda, and down to the municipality presidents and those levels, there has never been an order or an instruction to obstruct the power supply of Muslim Sarajevo. I'm not denying such incidents. This may have been a group of citizens or a group of soldiers. I'm not saying that this didn't happen but this is not a systemic obstruction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that the political authorities in Pale retained control over the decision to allow access to repair damaged transmission lines?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was director general of Elektroprivreda, I gave instructions and never received any instructions from the authorities at Pale. Those were very difficult times. It was war and these were really trifles for the Presidency of the RS to deal with. There was a general agreement that UNPROFOR in co-operation with both Elektroprivreda companies would form joint teams to access individual locations to make possible power supply for Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter number 24263, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Skoko, this is another UNPROFOR report from the 9th of February, 1994, a status report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we can go to page 3 under the title Electricity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: First of all, it's outlining how much electricity Sarajevo and Grbavica received for the week, 20 megawatts for Sarajevo and 7.5 megawatts for Grbavica. And then noted that this covers 10 per cent of the city's needs from before the war. But if we look at the third paragraph under the title electricity it says: "In January it was agreed to repair the line Reljevo-Buca Potok which is essential for the distribution of electricity to the people of Sarajevo. Still, clearance for this repair mission has not been given by Pale yet." Now, this document shows that although it was agreed that a repair would take place, it was the political authorities in the capital who prevented a repair from taking place; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the headquarters of Elektroprivreda was at Pale, so by "Pale," the headquarters of Elektroprivreda is meant here. Ours was a public institution and we were located at Pale and this has nothing to do with the political authorities of the RS.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Your Excellencies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask Madam Sutherland to show us where -- upon what her interpretation is that they didn't allow something because when I read the text I see that it says that electricity has not arrived yet and not that it was cut off. Line 24, prevented repair, but it does not follow from this document that we prevented anything, but rather that the approval or the clearance wasn't in yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: She referred to the passage that clearance has not given yet. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter number 24264, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Skoko, this is another UNPROFOR document dated the 27th of September, 1994, and if we can go to 1(b) on the first page, Electricity. And it says: "... repairs have begun on the Sarajevo network following Karadzic's agreement to clear the access of repair teams, provided UNPROFOR subsequently also addressed the problem of the eastern and northern Bosnia power lines, of particular interest to the Serb civilian populations." Now, this shows that it's the political leadership in Pale that gives the authorisation for repairs, in fact, to -- for access to the repair teams so that repairs can take place, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. No, it's not correct. I don't know if the UNPROFOR team happened to talk to President Karadzic. It may have been an individual instance. But repairs of the electric power network never required an approval of President Karadzic or the government or any instance above the Elektroprivreda.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that the Bosnian Serb authorities intentionally instructed -- obstructed the delivery of spare parts needed to repair the distribution network?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question for me?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: But whose report is this, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm asking you a question. The Bosnian Serb authorities intentionally obstructed the delivery of spare parts needed to repair the distribution network, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter number 24900, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we -- this is another UNPROFOR document dated the 11th of October, 1994. If we could go to page 2, please. And under the heading Electricity it says: "12.5 tonnes of transformer oil needed in Sarajevo for repairs to the distribution network, are blocked in Hrasnica (south of the airport) due to lack of clearance from the Bosnian Serbs (clearance would be granted if 50 per cent of it is given to the Serbs) ..." Now do you recall --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this information and I don't know who it was that supplied this, UNPROFOR or someone else. But I know that usually during the supply of spare parts and stuff the weapons could be smuggled. I don't know whether somebody from the Serb side demanded some oil. As I said, this information is unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Skoko --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I'm sure --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I'm sure that this demand for 50 per cent of the oil did not come from the authorities or the Elektroprivreda. That may have been an initiative of some local people or the municipality authorities, but as I said I have no information about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is another example of obstructing the power supply, isn't it? Because by withholding -- by blocking clearance, it then means that electricity supply cannot be fixed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with that. Even if we were to suppose that things were like that, I think that the Serbs at that moment had a fully legal demand. Both main transformer stations were on Serbian-controlled territory and they were -- they had been heavily shelled. Those were large transformer stations that needed much oil. Those were the transformer stations at Lukavica and at Blazuj. And the transformer stations in town were mostly small and they only needed 1/50th or 1/100th of the quantity the large ones needed. But it was very difficult to supply oil for the Blazuj transformer station. One litre of oil cost about 5 marks. Even if there was such a demand, of which as I said I'm not aware, it would have been a legitimate and legal demand made by Elektroprivreda.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Only this one, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, and the other documents that we -- 65 ter 24262 and 65 ter 26263 also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And 64?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, could you turn off your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. First of all, I would like to ask again that the Prosecution tender these documents by the time they're offered. I think by now everybody ought to know that they should do that. But having said that, I don't have any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll admit those four documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits P6270 through to Exhibits P6273 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Skoko, Mr. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb authorities used the restoration of utilities as a bargaining chip in the conflict, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So you're not aware that the Serb military forces prevented the restoration of utilities on conditions such as to compel the Bosnian Serb forces to stop fighting?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a legitimate demand. You can't expect people to go somewhere to die for the repair of a power line. The teams would not go out on the ground unless there was a cease-fire. In one such incident, six of our men were wounded while they were repairing power lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Skoko, you said there were never any decisions, orders, or any other instructions to cut off power supply to federal Sarajevo deliberately?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen such a decision, and I believe that there has never been one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 24253, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is another UNPROFOR document dated the 26th of May, 1995. And if we can go to page 3, please, it states --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you take a look at lines 20 to 22 on previous page. Is your question correctly reflected -- no, I'm sorry, the next question, lines 24 and 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's actually what she said but I had the same reaction when I heard it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I saw that too myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, I can put the question again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Skoko, a moment ago we were talking about the authorities using the restoration of utilities -- or the -- not restoring utilities as a bargaining chip in the conflict. And you said that you weren't aware of any documents where the Serb authorities were using the restoration or the non-restoration of utilities as a bargaining chip in the conflict. And I asked you whether you were -- and so I will ask you: The Bosnian Serb authorities did continue to insist that there would be no restoration of utilities until the fighting in the city had stopped?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have such orders or instructions, but even if there were some that would have been a legal and legitimate demand. Can you expect anybody in his right mind to go to the line of conflict to repair anything while there is fighting going on? It's not logical.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As you know, Dr. Skoko, there were meetings where there would be an agreement to stop the fighting so that a repair could go on. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so in these other instances, though, the Bosnian Serb authorities actually used it, the fact that they wouldn't do repairs, they wouldn't restore the utilities until fighting had stopped, they were using that as a bargaining chip to, in fact, have the Bosnians cease fighting against the Bosnian Serbs, trying to break out of the city?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct, not at all. This is nothing to do with what I stated. There has been no political pressure for the Muslims to stop fighting for Sarajevo. We're simply talking about the demand to cease fire in order to be able to repair infrastructure. This is nothing to do with political pressure and political blackmail.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you don't know that the Serb military authorities were of the same view that I just stated?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information about the behaviour of the Serb military authorities because I wasn't part of those structures. It is possible that some local authorities or local military groups obstructed, but I have no knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour and Mr. Karadzic, I would refer you to Exhibit P00896.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So, Dr. Skoko, getting back to this paragraph in your statement where you categorically state that nobody from the RS -- sorry, that there were never any decisions, orders, or any other instructions to cut off the power supply, and I wanted to take you to this document that we see on the screen, 65 ter number 24253. And if we look on page 3 it says, "This morning civil affairs...," and it's in the middle of the page now: "This morning civil affairs has been informed by SCS that the electricity supply to the city is cut. It appears that Pale authorities made a political decision to cut electricity supply along the Vogosca and Reljevo lines. If such situation persists Sarajevo will have no water soon." So this is a contemporaneous document at the time of the NATO air strikes which shows that it was deliberately cut, doesn't it? The document is dated the 26th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document doesn't show anything because it says "it seems." In other words, it is possible. It is possible that today is Wednesday, but no, it isn't, it's Monday. It says "it seems" here, but I state with full responsibility that there have never been such instructions from the high political level at Pale. Take a close look and you will see it only says "it seems."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: May I tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has not been recorded that Dr. Skoko said that he didn't know what kind of document this was. This wasn't recorded. The document was not introduced to him or us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm having said that, Mr. Skoko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, actually I did have an objection to this document, and that is I don't think -- first of all, the witness hasn't confirmed anything so the question is whether it contradicts him and that sentence, somebody's opinion, it appears that Pale authorities made a political decision which is a very subjective opinion as opposed to a contradictory fact, so I don't believe that this actually is a document that has probative value to contradict the witness and shouldn't be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does it not go to the weight at the end of the day, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it also goes to the weight but in terms of actually being a document which factually contradicts the witness I don't think it even meets the minimum standards of admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland, would you like to make any observation?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness categorically states that there were never any decisions, orders, or other instructions, and this is a document which shows that it was -- electricity was deliberately cut off or the -- perhaps, Your Honour, I can show another document and then if the two documents are read together it will make it clear that my -- the point that I'm trying to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter number 1D03405, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Skoko, this is another UNPROFOR document. It's dated the 28th of May, 1995. If we could go to e-court page 3. At point number 6 we can see -- we can see in point number 6 where they're summarising the events following the air strikes: "They have cut the water and electricity supplies to Sarajevo ..." If we could go to e-court page 6, please. So this document is two days after the earlier document that we just looked at. And at paragraph 17 it says: "Water and electricity supplies to Sarajevo city were cut by the Serbs as of Friday afternoon." And then it says -- talking about who controls the water supplies and then it says: "The small amount of electricity that exists would only be sufficient for emergencies such as government buildings and hospitals." So this document shows that the water and electricity supplies were cut off, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it does say that water and electricity supplies were cut off, but none of the items say whether that was a consequence of damage nor does it anywhere say that there were any orders issues from the leadership of Republika Srpska or Elektroprivreda of Republika Srpska or any station of the electricity board of Republika Srpska. So it doesn't say at all why the supply was cut off nor are any orders mentioned at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender these two documents. I think read together it makes it clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Skoko, while this document does not say it was specifically cut off by the decision of Serb authorities, but do you exclude such a possibility at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I exclude such a possibility. Not only was there no order issued from a high level of the authorities of Republika Srpska, I'm talking about the Presidency and the government, but not even from the level of the general manager and the management of the Elektroprivreda of Republika Srpska. This is what I claim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We don't have any objection to admission of this document which is factual in nature, but we maintain our objection to the first document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's a matter of weight that you will assign to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If we admit the second one, is there need to tender the first one?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It becomes a practicality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, the first one says that it appears Pale authorities made a political decision to cut the electricity supply along Vogosca and Reljevo lines, and that's on the 26th of May. And then on the 28th of May it simply says they cut the water and electricity supplies in Sarajevo, so I think you need to have the two documents to make the link.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the contextual situation we'll admit both of them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits P6274 and Exhibit P6275 respectively.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Skoko, you know that Vogosca line feeds into Sarajevo 2 which is the Veselici line and that the Reljevo line feeds Sarajevo 7 which is the Buca Potok line, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Also, just in relation to the cutting off of water, water-supply relies on electrical pumps, doesn't it? So if there's no electricity, there's no running water, is there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, apart from one part of the waterworks up in Bistrik.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the witness please repeat the last part of his answer because the interpreters couldn't hear him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Skoko, could you repeat your last part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a small waterworks in Bistrik which could supply a part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, how much more would you need to conclude your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I would just like to put one document and two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. 65 ter number 24254, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Skoko, another UNPROFOR document dated the 31st of July, 1995. And if we -- it's a weekly situation report. If we could go to the last page, please, in e-court page 7. And under section (F) Daily Life under Utilities, it states there: "Serb authorities in western Sarajevo, now willing to talk to their Bosnian counterparts, said that they cut off the water, electricity, and gas supplies in late May to 'punish the Muslims' for their offensive around the city." Now, this document dated July 1995 is referring back to the fact that electricity was cut off in May 1995. And this is just another example of deliberately cutting off the water-supply, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This does not confirm your thesis. I suppose that this is part of Sarajevo between Vogosca and Sarajevo. So this is the section that was involved in combat operations all the time and this does not confirm the thesis that there were orders from a high level to cut off electricity supply, though I do not dispute the fact that perhaps something may have been destroyed by the local fighters and so on. That's possible. However, that does not confirm your main thesis.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: First of all, Vogosca is in the north of Sarajevo. We're talking here about Serb authorities in western Sarajevo. But in any event, it is another example, is it not, of deliberately cutting off the supply of electricity by the Bosnian Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it's not the local authorities which are mentioned here. This could perhaps be the local fighters but certainly not the local Serb authorities. No order, no instructions or anything of the kind was issued or is mentioned here. Now I cannot be aware of each individual incident. There were individual incidents along the front line and I do not dispute that; however, that was not the rule.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Skoko. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you tendering this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you remind me, by western Sarajevo what does it refer to, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Western Sarajevo is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I mean the authorities in western Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can -- that would be -- it could be authorities in Ilidza and/or the SRK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I will leave it at that. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please return the document that was last on the screen so that we can see it again and the same page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P6276, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Skoko, I would ask you to look at the last paragraph under Schools. What was their estimate of the number of people living there, the population, and what is your estimate?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Schools was not a topic for cross-examination. We were dealing specifically with electricity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, school is mentioned in the document admitted. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was going to leave it to Dr. Karadzic to explain to you where he's going with this because I myself don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you follow, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellencies. This piece of information is just located under the subtitle Schools and I'm interested in the population estimate, 300.000. This was an estimate which was served up by the Muslim side obviously because Dr. Skoko said around 200.000 and so this is not 600.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. If you would like to deal with the population, I will allow the question. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Skoko, I wanted to ask you to look at their estimate here and how different it is from the data you had that were based on the census. So are we talking about 600.000 inhabitants of Sarajevo or is it just the city proper?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, these are not my information. These are the official information from the statistics bureau of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that in the four municipalities in the city there were almost 200.000 Muslims, but that was even not the complete figure. The figure was somewhat smaller.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned a small waterworks on Bistrik and was there some free fall on the Serbian side with water that was flowing into Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the water that was flowing into the Serbian Sarajevo or the greater part of the water was flowing down from Pale. As you said it was a free fall from Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Serbian side ever cut off this flow of water coming from Bistrica or anywhere else where there was a free fall? You were in the government. Was it ever suggested or ordered or did it ever happen that the water, except for Bacevo where electricity was necessary, that somewhere where electricity was not necessary water was cut off and there was no supply to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the information that ever such an information was issued or that there were ever any instructions given to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure if this is the same document, probably it is. No, 1D03405. Can we please have a look at that one. We would need page 3, please. Paragraph 6 to which Madam Sutherland referred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will read it out to you in the English language so that it would be interpreted to you. It will be better than I would do it: [In English] "Events following the air strikes have so far resulted in about 80 dead and over 160 injured. Further, the Serbs are subjecting 325 UNPROFOR personnel ...," and so on and so on. [Interpretation] Do you remember this bombing from the end of May 1995, and was this a bombing that had an impact on the electricity supply infrastructure?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, just as any other bombing it has to -- it caused some damage. I do not have the precise information about what was damaged because I was not in Pale at that moment. The Elektroprivreda was located in Bijeljina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please see the next page which Madam Prosecutor referred to and quoted something from it. I think it's the last page of the document. No, the penultimate page I suppose then. I cannot find on which page it is, but the document said that 80 per cent of electricity and water was supplied via the Serbian territory. Is that information that is close to your knowledge? Was it more or was it less?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know what was the amount of water exactly. I do not have this information, but during 1992-1995 of the total amount of electricity 55 -- or actually 550 was coming through the Serbian territory and 42 through the Serbian territory. So 42 per cent from Serbian territory and 8 per cent, if I'm not mistaken, was coming from across the territories that were not under the Serb control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now have a look at -- I apologise to the interpreters. Could we please once again see 24900, probably it has been assigned a different number now. It is a document that was discussed on page 15. Next page, please. That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please see this under Electricity. I will read it: [In English] "The city of Sarajevo now receives about 20 megawatts, while the minimum requirement is said to be 60 megawatts ..." [Interpretation] Is this the calculation for the whole city or did they only calculate for the inner city?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whose calculations these are. Unfortunately, I really could not confirm this. However, first when we talk about megawatts, it is unusual to calculate the needs in megawatts rather than in kilowatts per hour. However, 60 megawatts would in any case be something inappropriate for this relevant period. 60 megawatts would really be quite a lot for that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please have a look at what is said in the further text: [In English] "This means that priority areas receive electricity 24 hours a day, while most of the city receives electricity a few hours per day." [Interpretation] Would even these 20 megawatts, as they termed them, cover the priorities around-the-clock, whereas there were restrictions imposed on the population. And could you please tell the Chamber how frequent were the restrictions and under what circumstances in war time and peace time restrictions have to be introduced?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know how they distributed the electricity and what they use it for, it's difficult to comment on that. But I can say, for example, that at the time in -- for the most part of 1992 and 1993 and when we talk about restrictions, most of the restrictions were in the part Republika Srpska including 20 Serb municipalities in Krajina where on every seven days there would be four hours or less during which the electricity was supplied and that lasted for almost a year and a half. You know that at the time 12 babies perished in Banja Luka. That is to say that the situation with regard to supply of electricity in Sarajevo not to mention the megawatts or kilowatts per hour were far, far better by comparison to other Serb-populated areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And under Water down on the screen, can you please have a look at that as well because of electricity. It says there: [In English] "Water supply relies on electrical pumps. The Bacevo pumping station, which is the main station for Sarajevo, has been receiving low levels of electricity recently because of problems with the Vogosca-Reljevo line." [Interpretation] Is it true that the pumps from Bacevo were the main station for the supply of Sarajevo and that they depended on electricity supply as it's stated here?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't have the information about water-supply. I am not expert enough to comment on that, how much electricity these water-pumps consumed. However, based on the information I heard from a colleague who was in charge of that, the problem of Bacevo was mostly that there were cut-offs in the power lines because they were shelled by Muslim shells from Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive reports that the Muslim side shelled these key transformer stations in Blazuj? And were these stations in Serbian territory? If they were, would Serbs shell their own transformer stations?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I cannot give you an exact reference. I don't remember the month. It was during 1993 when the Serb side even offered that the power line should be repaired and that electricity supply should be provided for Hrasnica which was then under Muslim control. Electricity was then supplied even up to Igman. After that, the Muslim side shelled from up there when the three main transformer stations were hit at the Blazuj transformer station. After that the whole city including the Serb and Muslim-populated side with the exception of small part of the Sarajevo populated -- of the Serb-populated Sarajevo was left without electricity for one month. I think this was a crazy act of the Muslim side as if they deliberated wanted to cause a humanitarian catastrophe in Sarajevo, a humanitarian disaster, so they could manipulate it thereafter. It was not justified and not caused by anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a look at 24262 for a minute so that Dr. Skoko would be allowed to complete his sentence, or rather, to read the entire sentence to him. The document has been assigned a new number now, but it was 24262.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we need the following page -- or, just a moment. Excuse me. No, electricity is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will read it out to you. You were read this: [In English] "Serbs denied any access to the repair location on the line which is supplying the town (Reljevo/Vogosca)." [Interpretation] And it goes on: [In English] "Fierce fighting and shelling have provoked a lot of cuts and damages in the northern area of Sarajevo." [Interpretation] What is your knowledge about the effect this heavy fighting and shelling between Sarajevo and Vogosca had on the structure of electricity transmission?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is only natural that transmission and distribution would be affected by fighting. That was the root cause of these problems. Distribution is affected, transmission is affected, small transformer stations are destroyed, so the entire system cannot work. I've already said that when one segment of the system fails then the entire system can no longer function. It is only natural when fighting is going on these facilities cannot be repaired and time is needed to repair it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Skoko. You mentioned that there has to be a balance so that things could function. Electricity transmission and electricity distribution, is there a difference and who was responsible for what? The Trial Chamber should be made aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, please do try to explain what you meant by that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned production, transmission, distribution, and so on. Just explain the difference between transmission and distribution, is that the same service?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, these are two different services. Transmission goes from production to major transformer stations, and then major transformer stations transform voltage and then smaller users receive electricity afterwards. Distribution can involve several, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And which level? Which service is affected by the local factor and which is affected by the central factor?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as distribution is concerned, it can be affected by the local factor. However, in war time it can affect both because transmission goes through municipalities. In peacetime local, or rather, municipal organs should not have any effect on electricity transmission; however, the situation becomes a bit more complicated in war time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I see the time but I do need some 10 or 12 minutes to complete this witness's examination. So perhaps after the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We shall take a break for half an hour and resume at three past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, if I may interrupt Mr. Karadzic's re-examination for one moment. You asked me at page 27 who the authorities were in western Sarajevo, and I think it was a brain freeze and I could only put it down to the leg, but I forgot to mention Novi Grad and the Reljevo power station which is in the territory of the SRK. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Skoko, to the best of your knowledge, did I interfere in supply-related matters; and if I did interfere, did I interfere for the sake of making things better or worse?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Karadzic, I never received any instruction from you and not only not from you, an instruction that would mean obstruction in terms of making the electric supply of Sarajevo worse. If you did not give us support in terms of material and other support, that is to say appealing to the government to repair the facilities and to possibly improve production, transmission, and distribution, you never carried out any activity that would be considered obstruction.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D5312, could we please have a look at that in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just a moment ago this was mentioned, local government. It was also mentioned in cross-examination. So I would like to ask you -- actually, this isn't it in English. Yes, now we have the right document. Could we please take a look at this. The 9th of August, 1993, the then-Prime Minister Lukic says: "Pursuant to Article 29, paragraph 3 of the Law on State Administration ... and the order of the president of Republika Srpska, I hereby order. "The presidents of the Executive Committees of the Municipal Assemblies, the chiefs of public security stations and commanders of the units of the Army of Republika Srpska ..." Then now we see paragraphs 1, 2, 3: "Enable the unobstructed passage of regularly announced humanitarian aid convoys and UNPROFOR teams ..." And then we see what the other two paragraphs say. How does this fit into your knowledge regarding the activity of the government and the president of the republic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This fully falls in line with what I said. This is, at any rate, affirmative for the Elektrodistribucija of Republika Srpska to ensure normal -- well, not exactly normal but the best possible supply of water, gas, and electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can is this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3328, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D07542, could we please have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Two days later let us see how the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps reacts to all of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Does Mr. Karadzic have a question for the witness before he brings up the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Skoko, to the best of your knowledge, such orders of the prime minister were they taken seriously and were they implemented in the field?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you for the most part yes, but there were obstructions too. I have to say that when the war started when I became director general of Elektrodistribucija or Republika Srpska I encountered major problems in placing under my command part of the Elektrodistribucija in Krajina, because some of the SAOs had been formed and then some parts of the Elektrodistribucija behaved rather autonomously. So I'm not ruling out the possibility of obstructions of the decisions taken by the prime minister and also the president of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now look at the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Two days after that order that order is being referred to. It says here on the basis of the order of the prime minister of Republika Srpska and now it is being elaborated. It becomes an executive order to the units. And can we have the next page paragraph 8 -- actually paragraph 8 starts on this page in English so can we scroll down in English. However, in Serbian we need the next page. Paragraph 8 says: "Offer assistance to the civilian organs of government for ensuring the flow of electric power and gas to the Sarajevo city area, to the extent that organisation of the military permits." You said that things did depend on the fighting that was going on. How do you see this reaction of the corps commander two days after that order had been issued?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that it is in accordance with your order and what was up to the military was to stop fighting in order to enable access to the lines so that repairs could be carried out. And then also to remove mines in possible minefields in order to make it possible to repair the transmission lines and other facilities that were down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Me or witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Interpreters didn't hear your saying, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked whether this could be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3329, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Skoko, what was the position of civilian authorities in general and the directorate in terms of not providing power, water, et cetera, in terms of international law?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, civilian authorities - and I include the top echelons of the government and Elektrodistribucija of Republika Srpska - we were always prepared to a maximum within the realm of the possible to provide those supplies of electricity that could have been provided. I was not aware of a single obstruction of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat the number and pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D40031.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, this is in the English language so I'm going to read it out. This is the SRNA report. It says that SRNA is authorised to publish the following letter of the president of the Presidency of Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, addressed to UNPROFOR and it says: [In English] "Sirs. "In the war being waged in the area of BH against Serbian people, it is evident that some methods, forbidden by all international conventions, are being used. Cutting electric current and phone lines to the Serbian territory by Muslims is the latest example. This is just one in the series of similar provocations directed to everything that is Serbian. We have to emphasise that the Serbian side has done nothing similar to that. We are asking from UNPROFOR to use its authority and engage in stopping such incidents and to make pressure upon the other side in order to alleviate mutual distrust and hatred, which is the essential basis for establishing peace." [Interpretation] How does this fit into your own knowledge concerning my position and the position of the authorities of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That fully tallies with what I stated a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again this is an example of putting leading question. The question you put before you showed this document has -- had nothing to do with the content of this document. Please bear that in mind, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Excellency, I did put a question in terms of how we viewed that in the context of international norms. I did ask about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This fully fits into all international norms, and therefore it fits into my previous answers; namely, that no obstructions were ever carried out in terms of supplying electricity to the population of Sarajevo in respect of orders, decisions, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lines 20 to 23, I asked what our position was in terms of international law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson will tell you how to put your foundational question. Please bear in mind leading questions will reduce the probative value of the evidence elicited from the witness. We'll receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3330, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was suggested here several times that we obstructed repairs of the grid around Sarajevo. Do you know about this? Did we intentionally damage anything and did we obstruct repairs from the level of government and the system as such?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot rule out individual excesses committed by soldiers in the field, that can never be ruled out. However, as far as supply is concerned and as far as repairs are concerned and this overall positive activity in terms of making the electricity system function, I never received any orders or instructions against that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how the other side acted in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: A moment ago I gave two very specific examples when an attempt was made to supply electricity to Hrasnica. They intentionally -- well, I don't know whether it was intentional or whatever, but they shelled the transformer station of Blazuj and that's why all of Sarajevo remained without any electricity and I could give many other examples. So when electricity was supposed to come from the hydro-electric power-plant of Visegrad to Muslim Sarajevo, Muslim soldiers cut that line in order to obstruct the power supply for the Pretis Vogosca factory. These are two very specific examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I have a question of language. On page 10 in relation to that report on supplies for Sarajevo you said that that was a manipulation. Can you tell us on the basis of what you conclude that that is a manipulation and do you have any explanation of this bilingual presentation of supplies?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, please, what did this question have to do with?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 10 you were shown a document, a Muslim report about power supplies in Sarajevo and it was bilingual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Show the document and ask him why he thought it was part of manipulation. It was annual report of Elektroprivreda.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I don't know what the number is. I would appreciate it if Ms. Sutherland could tell us the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah, yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Exhibit P6269, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please. Further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the whole you do see the introductory part as well. What led you to believe that this was a manipulation, as you said on page 10?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see what the quantities involved are here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think -- sorry to interrupt. I think Mr. Karadzic wants page 10 which -- of this document which was admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If it was displayed, yes. In the city of Sarajevo -- actually, it's the fourth paragraph from the top of the page, the supply of Sarajevo by electricity was provided, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us what you know about this.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't have any knowledge about there being 53 days without electricity in Sarajevo uninterrupted. I said that the period of the end of December 1992 and January 1993 was the longest uninterrupted period when the Blazuj transformer station was shelled. So this figure of 53 days does not correspond to the facts. As for 1993 that for 140 days the city did not have any power, I believe that this does not correspond to the factual situation because in 1993, as compared to 1992, the power supply had been improved and you can see that from the tables that I attached when I was making my presentation provided by the electric transmission company of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There is a table there in terms of the power supplied in 1993, and that shows that power supply in 1993 was significantly increased compared to 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you said "manipulation," what would the motive be? Why? Why do you think that this was manipulation presenting the situation in this way?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably to create an impression of a greater humanitarian catastrophe and the extent to which the population of Sarajevo suffered because of power shortages. I'm not denying that there were major problems in respect of power supply, but I can assert that the population would not have been in the situation that they were in had the use of electric energy been more rational.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Last question. On page 3 I'm afraid that this has to do with idiomatic differences. Did you say that you were not doing anything -- are you saying that you were unemployed or underdeployed or what?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SKOKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I did have a job but I was not sufficiently being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Skoko.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your evidence, Dr. Skoko. And on behalf of this Tribunal and the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could very quickly raise a follow-up to an issue I mentioned last Thursday. I indicated to Mr. Robinson and I would indicate this to the Court, that was the continuing concern over documents considered to be or intended to be used as associated exhibits or other exhibits for statements that were not translated. And at that time I explained the nature of the problem to the Court, both in this particular instance and as it had persisted in other circumstances for quite some time. And I underscored the Prosecution's many efforts to prevent that from delaying the proceedings in any way on -- and Mr. Robinson also commended the Prosecution for its efforts in that regard. On Friday Mr. Robinson asked me to advise whether under the circumstances and in light of his indication that understanding the situation he would not object to any requests by the Prosecution to continuance, whether we intended to do so. I advised him that we would proceed but that I would want to indicate to the Court the efforts it took by the Prosecution to do so. And I mention that not to invite further commendation from the Court or Mr. Robinson, but simply to note that this really is straining the Prosecution's resources at some point and notwithstanding our desire to do everything possible to keep it impeding the proceedings. We will not be in a position to move forward and some delay will result. And the answer will not be simply moving the next witness forward or taking a witness from further on in the week because that will only shift the preparation problem, obviously. So I bring that to the Court's attention. I hope very much that it won't arise again, but in the event it does I thought the Court needed to know the backdrop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. I fully understand. The Chamber appreciates your genuine effort for the smooth conduct of the trial. Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Skiljevic. Good morning to you. Would you make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Skiljevic, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of procedure and evidence that we have here at the Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question.
