But in that situation the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any case save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Skiljevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Skiljevic.

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just please let us observe a break between question and answer, and I would also ask you to reply at a moderate pace so we needn't repeat everything and so that everything may be recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see Exhibit 1D7913 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skiljevic, please look at the screen. Do you see your statement on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you read and sign the statement?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: I read and signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please let us see the last page. Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to ask you the same questions live today, would your replies be essentially the same as those in the statement?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: They would be the same replies as in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I seek to tender this statement and some other documents. Some of them I will lead live especially those that haven't been translated and I will have some additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I apologise for the state of the associated exhibits with this witness. We made our best efforts to have the documents translated and had sent them to translation, but there was a large number of them and not all of them were completed on time. So we are offering 28 associated exhibits, 27 of which are not on our Rule 65 ter list and we would ask that they be added as we hadn't interviewed the witness at the time that list was submitted. And I can list for you either the ones that we're seeking to tender or the ones that we're not seeking to tender that were on our list, whichever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't know how to -- I have a list of 39 items. So it means that you dropped 12 items?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. The difference is that there are some items that have already been admitted and other items where we have no translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's deal with the 92 ter statement first. Could you take a look at paragraph 19 and 38 -- no, that's okay. It's not identical. Fine. Shall we take a look at 20 and 37, para 20 and another example is 21 and 40. The last couple -- the last batch seems to be identical except for the passage that it was discussed earlier. Twenty-one and 40. It would not be a big deal even if there are some duplicative paragraphs, but please bear in mind in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any objection, Ms. Gustafson? Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. To the statement, no, there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3331, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So can I hear from you for the items you have objection to?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm not sure to what extent they overlap with the Defence's decision on what they will be tendering under 92 ter and not, but the documents to which we object because there is no translation are 1D06847 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think they are going to --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- be led live in my understanding. Do you confirm that, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay so then there are only two other objections, 1D50014, referenced at paragraph 43. The exhibit appears to consist of two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly. It's 1D50014.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In which there are allegedly two documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's what appears to be the case and the comments at paragraph 43 seem to concern only the first of those documents. So our objection is to the second of the documents which is the second page in the B/C/S. Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- I take it there will be no objection to the admission of the first one?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we can -- we don't object to admitting that and Dr. Karadzic can lead the second one live if he wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. And your next objection, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: My next and my last is 1D50021, referenced at paragraph 50. The comments at paragraph 50, in our submission, don't actually explain what this document is and that is not self-evident from the document itself. So in our submission this is another document that should be covered live. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. That does not form an indispensable and inseparable part of the document. Before I deal with some specific items, can I have a general question for you, Mr. Robinson or Mr. Karadzic, that there are many documents that relates to the time-frame after the incident that allegedly took place in KP Dom in the indictment. To be more specific, the indictment deals with the time-frame from May until October of 1992, but many of the documents are dealing with events in 1993, 1994, or even 1995. So how are these documents relevant to your case, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Excellencies, this is a penitentiary institution and we see how the authorities treated detained persons. Moreover, civilians are also hosted there, civilians waiting to go to the Muslim-controlled part of the city. If the indictment is about a systemic approach, then this is something to be taken into consideration. And the prison was only established in the summer of 1992, a few months after the start of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While I can understand -- but the Chamber is of the view that we will not admit the following documents: 1D50025 and 1D50026. This deals with either shelling nearly three years after the indictment or similar things. As such, the Chamber is of the view they are not relevant. And finally -- the same goes to the 1D50029. So we'll not admit those three. And finally, as regards 1D50028, the Chamber is also of the view that does not form an indispensable and inseparable part of the statement. Further, I'm not sure it is one of the documents you are tendering. It is not consistent with our practice to admit a third party's statement as an associated exhibit. But I will check with the Registrar whether he can follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise for not rising earlier, but I had to remind myself of the precise wording of the indictment which I've just looked up. The Prosecution's operative indictment has a footnote to the schedule for Kula prison under Schedule C and the footnote states that the KP Dom Butmir served as a detention facility until at least 28 October 1994. So the Prosecution has extended the time-period that it initially alleged for the operation of this prison. I would add that it's the Prosecution's case that the Kula prison does form an integral part of the exchange commission functioning and process and has relevance to that issue as well which persisted throughout the war. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you indeed. I would like Registrar to liaise with the parties outside the courtroom to - how to say? -- to arrange the documents to be admitted as associated exhibits. And the associated exhibits -- how many items are there, Mr. Robinson, according to your calculation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, there were 28 associated exhibits that we were offering. You've taken away four of those that we intended to offer, so that would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Four or five?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, by my count those three that you mentioned as being irrelevant and the one that you mentioned is not an inseparable part of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And Ms. Gustafson raised another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, there were two objections from Ms. Gustafson that you've sustained those, so that's true. So there would be 22 associated exhibits being offered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be helpful. So those will be admitted and be given number in due course. Very well. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read out the summary of Mr. Skiljevic's statement in English, after which I will ask some additional questions. [In English] Mr. Soniboje Skiljevic was deputy manager and by the end of 1992 he became manager in Butmir penal and correctional facility in Kula near Sarajevo. He stayed on that position until the end of 1995. On 6th of April, 1992, Mr. Skiljevic arrived at work at the KPD to be told that the convicts had been released on the orders of the KPD chief, Fadil Kreho. At that time, Mr. Skiljevic was a counsellor at the KPD. Tanks were seen that day about 100 metres away from the gate of the KPD. The next day when Mr. Skiljevic returned to KPD -- returned, the KPD had been taken over by the army. The war situation was increasingly deteriorating and he learned that Muslim extremists were threatening to kill him he decided to flee with his family. The army put his wife and children on to trucks and transported them to safe Serbian territory. Mr. Skiljevic returned to work on the farm at the KPD and soon after he did, military police moved in the KPD. The movements of the workers were restricted and records were kept of the comings and goings. On 30th of June, 1992, Butmir KPD became a closed institution and Soniboje Skiljevic was appointed chief of the administrations department at the service for the correction of convicted persons. After this the police then vacated the premises. It was explained to all employees that the prisoners were to be treated extremely humanely. He was unaware of the grounds for the detention of the prisoners as that was within the jurisdiction of the military. He was only concerned with the operations and prison records were kept. Prisoners were taken by the army outside of the KPD to complete work. Soniboje Skiljevic does not know where the prisoners were taken; however, he is aware that the prisoners did not complain about how they were being treated and most requested voluntarily to be sent to work. All activities Soniboje Skiljevic carried out were reported to the MUP and military security organs. The employees at the KPD were told that the people staying were prisoners of war and that they should be taken care of, fed, and given medical assistance, not to be mistreated. The prisoners were served three meals a day after the establishment of the Butmir KPD. There were no complaints about the quantity or quality of food. Those completing labour were given a further light meal. The same food was given to employees and officials at the KPD and those with dietary requirements were catered for. None of the prisoners went hungry. Medical assistance was provided to the prisoners in a timely and appropriate manner. Prisoners were often referred to other medical centres of the hospital depending on the illness or injury. The building where prisoners of war were kept had -- have been furnished with mattresses, beds, pillows, and two blankets per person. The block was heated by a boiler; however, this was destroyed in a Muslim shell attack and therefore furnaces were set up to heat every room. Soniboje Skiljevic categorically claims that during the period when he was the acting KPD warden, the prisoners of war and other prisoners were not subjected to torture, mistreatment, physical or other abuse, humiliation, and the like. He also maintains that there were no women with children at the KPD. The prisoners of war were visited on a number of occasions by the International Red Cross who brought them further provisions and letters. Also the KPD was visited by Radovan Karadzic, an international representative, and many foreign reporters and journalists. They observed that -- the living conditions of the prisoners, dining area, and quality of food as well as speaking to the prisoners. Some prisoners were killed or wounded in the shelling of the area around the KPD and the farm. The KPD was shelled several times from the Muslim positions during the war. A number of prisoners were also killed at labour sites outside the KPD by shells and sniper bullets fired from the Muslim side. In December 1992 Butmir KPD housed 130 prisoners of war from the military detention camp at Manjaca. Soniboje Skiljevic raised the issue of the housing of prisoners of war to the Government of Republika Srpska but no solution was found to this issue. [Interpretation] This was a short summary. Let me now ask some questions to Mr. Skiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when I visited the Kula prison and how often was I there, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: You visited the Kula prison on the 9th of August, 1992. You were with a delegation and a significant number of international journalists and domestic journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember who accompanied me, what kind of delegation it was?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Paddy Ashdown was with you and other high dignitaries. There were about 60 to 70 journalists from all over the world and cameramen too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there anyone from the Red Cross in that delegation?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were people from the Red Cross and other international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that visit announced to you; and if so, how long in advance?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was a Saturday. The then-warden, Mr. Lalovic, was not present because he had left to his -- to the town where he was born to visit his parents. Mr. Mandic was there instead and an hour or an hour and a half before your arrival we were informed. We also slept at the KPD because we had fled Sarajevo and didn't have other accommodation. So we were on the premises. Minister Mandic only said that there will be high-ranking delegation to visit the KPD. We didn't know that you would be there, but then around 3.00 you arrived with the journalists and other guests.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that occasion, just like before, did you get or did you hear any objections or suggestions from Mr. Ashdown or the Red Cross? Did they complain to anything as being irregular or not in line with the regulations?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: There were no objections from the delegation. They visited the sleeping areas of the prisoners of war, or rather, they went to the building because both prisoners of war and convicts of Serbian ethnicity slept in -- on the same premises. We didn't get any complaints to their safety or their nutrition and we were often visited by the Red Cross. I could even say once in two months. They talked to the prisoners of war that [as interpreted] our presence, not even the police could be present during those interviews and they would write down messages for the detainees' families and they also gave them cigarettes and clothes and so on. After interviewing the prisoners of war they always met me who was the chief of the institution. And from the day I became warden, that is, the 16th of December, 1992, there you had no objections about the conditions or anything else at the KPD.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were they able to talk to journalists and Lord Ashdown without the presence of the KP Dom staff on this one occasion?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: They could freely talk to anyone, the journalists or Mr. Paddy Ashdown or personally with you. Whoever wanted to do so could talk freely without any problems and state whatever they wanted to say at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During this visit, did any of them inform me about a criminal offence or object or complain about the way they were being treated?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no one did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you -- I'm waiting for the interpretation. Did you know what my position and the position of government organs was about the way the prisoners of war and the prisoners were to be treated in accordance with the Penal Code, if they were prisoners who committed other crimes?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Your position was - and that was emphasised to us - that we had to take care about security, that we had to act in a decent manner, that we could provide everything in terms of food and everything else to the prisoners of war because they were there temporarily and they were actually under the jurisdiction of the exchange committees and on any day they could be sent to a different part of Sarajevo or somewhere else, wherever the exchange commission decided they were to be sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement you mentioned there were also civilians who were waiting to cross over into Sarajevo. You mention a village from the Rogatica area. Can you tell us, if you remember, did you have civilians from the Vrbanja village which administratively belonged to the Sokolac municipality but borders the Rogatica municipality. I'm talking about September 1992 -- excuse me, 1994 and 1995, that was Vrbanja.

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: As our co-operation was continuous with the exchange commission and as early on at the beginning of the war it was called the exchange bureau. In 1993 the commission for exchange was formed by the Government of Republika Srpska and it was chaired by Dragan Bulajic. Whoever needed to be exchanged was exchanged through the commission. The chairman of the commission and other persons could not influence any exchanges. As for the civilians that you asked me about, the agreement was between the Muslim and Serbian civilian and military authorities that for security reasons and on request of these persons to be transferred to Sarajevo so that they would join their families, those persons were transferred from Rogatica to the KP Dom. They were isolated in a different wing from other persons, both Serbs, Muslims, and Croats, that is to say persons who had already been accommodated at the KP Dom before then. UNHCR and other international organisations saw to it that these persons would be transported on a daily basis in their vehicles whenever the conditions were met across the Brastvo Jedinstvo bridge into Sarajevo. So these persons would stay with us between five days and two months, in effect until all such persons were exchanged. And the commission for exchange was solely responsible for this, and this was called joining or linking up the families.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they enjoy the same treatment as prisoners of war or were they detained there on the basis of criminal reports?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: They were separated from prisoners of war and they were treated in a decent manner such as everyone else who was accommodated at the KP Dom. We treated them humanely and in accordance with the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who provided food to them and how did you manage to do that? Did you manage to support them? Did anyone help you to feed these people?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Even before the war and immediately after the break-out of the armed conflict, the KP Dom had an economy unit which was called Privrednik. So during the war it was set up on your orders because your order was to organise economic activity in all enterprises. We produced eggs for consumption. We had around 25.000 egg-laying hens. We had some pigs as well. We also grew vegetables. We had workshops and so on. This was the only semi-open type of the KP Dom in Bosnia-Herzegovina. As the warden, I requested from the high commissariat and the ICRC and the Government of Republika Srpska and I always received positive answers and a sufficient contingent of food for the needs of this institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that the time that people spent there varied. What was the interest of the KP Dom to have these people stay shorter or longer and what would the duration of their stay depend on?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: The KP Dom had no interest whatsoever. It was only a burden for us, a burden for the institution to have these people staying with us even if they stayed for a single day because we had sufficient people who were under investigation by the military organs and others who were under investigation or who were punished by the district court, but they stayed with us because that was the agreement of two commissions. Whenever the security situation allowed for them to cross over without any hindrance into Sarajevo, they would leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned in your statement, for example, in paragraph 21, there were some problems with treatment and providing medication. Can you tell us how you resolved such issues?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: We had good co-operation with the Kasindol hospital which is located close to the KP Dom, about 3 kilometres away. We also had military medical outpost in Lukavica about 300 metres away, then the military hospital Koran, one department, then the Sokolac military hospital. In all these institutions we treated the prisoners of war who had been sentenced or just detained. Some of the detainees and prisoners of war were in the Blazuj facility that could accommodate around 70 persons. These persons were treated at the Zice hospital in Blazuj. We received the medication and everything else from the Kasindol hospital and from the military hospital. And as even from before the war the medical service that we had was quite developed. We had our own medical staff and a makeshift supply of medication. We were provided great assistance by the International Red Cross, the health department. Practically every month they would come to visit us. They would perform the triage and also send us some medications and medical supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I did not understand whether document 1D06847 has been admitted with paragraph 40, or should I call it up in connection with paragraph 21?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this not one of the documents where the English translation is lacking?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes. Then I would like to call up this document, 1D6847. If we could please see it in e-court so that I could ask the witness to tell us what this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at this document and tell us what it represents as we still do not have the translation. You may even read out the text if you prefer.

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: "The Ministry of Justice, correctional facility Butmir, number so an so, date the 16th of December, 1993, Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the 4th Medical Battalion, subject: Request for borrowing medication. As at the moment we have more than 320 [as interpreted] prisoners of war and people who are under investigation by military and civilian authorities as well as people who are sentenced by civilian authorities at the moment and we are unable to provide medication to all of them. We address you in order to provide us with a contingent for our makeshift medical supplies depot."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was "220" and in interpretation we heard "320."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you are asking to borrow medical supplies from the medical battalion of RSK. Did you receive that when you requested medical supplies in this form?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we requested from Dr. Ranko Subotic to provide this, as he worked then at the military hospital Koran and on several occasions he also came to do check-ups of prisoners and also to see what were the conditions under which they lived and worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please scroll down so that you can tell us what is written in hand above his signature. No, scroll up rather than scroll down.

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: It says "approved," and there's a signature and we can see that it says Dr. Ranko Subotic, hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3354, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement you say that the premises in the KP Dom, the facilities as a whole, were satisfactory. It was satisfactory for what number of detainees, can you tell us anything about that? How many toilets and bathrooms were there? How big were the rooms and so on?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: The KP Dom was renovated in 1988 and two new buildings were made including all the necessities, everything that was necessary for persons who were sentenced. Up until the war no investigations were conducted and persons who were under investigation were not accommodated there. Only persons who had been sentenced for petty crimes. At the Butmir KP Dom, as Kula is actually called, more than 450 detainees could be accommodated, and at the department which was outside of the KP Dom Butmir in Blazuj, Ilidza, or as it was popularly known Igman, it could accommodate 80 detainees. The facility that was used immediately at the beginning, we all called it D2 facility or D2 building, had 14 rooms with toilet and shower blocks in one wing and 14 in another. So 28 in total. We also had other facilities there, three other facilities, workshops. And across the road from the KP Dom at a distance of about 300 metres we also had our economy unit called Privrednik where we had facilities used to produce eggs for consumption. There was a restaurant and makeshift depots. Within the KP Dom we had workshop and we used to make concrete items. The administration building included the medical service and an infirmary. So at any moment we could receive 450 persons and around 17 other department outside of the KP Dom. So 470 persons on the whole if we did not want it to be crowded. As for the D2 wing, in the left wing we held persons who were the category of captured persons or prisoners, prisoners of war, and in the other wing on the ground floor there were sentenced persons and on the floor there were persons who were under jurisdiction of the army and who were being investigated into. Across the road from these buildings, before the war we had the reception department, that is to say where they would be processed by professionals once they were admitted and where more than 100 persons could be accommodated. In this new building, the other one I mean, we had rooms where the detainees could spend the day, a library and some other rooms.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D5009.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You talk about the facilities that you had at your disposal in paragraph 34 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please have 1D50009 [Realtime transcript read in error "1D5009"]. We do not need the statement. We need this one, 1D50009.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're looking at 5009 so you need to put another 0 in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skiljevic, are you familiar with this document? I see down here the stamp of the Tribunal. Do you know what this document is?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a copy of the cadastral plan of the KP Dom. The document was drawn up in 1996 and the document with all the accompanying documents was seized from the KP Dom in 2003 and sent here to the international Tribunal at The Hague. All the documents that were found at the KP Dom we received an order from the Ministry of Justice that we had to hand over all the documents from the war-time period to investigators. So they came to visit us. They photocopied everything and they marked all the documents and sent them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what it is that we see here. Are these some collective bathrooms, sinks? Where is this?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: This is at D2, the facility that I spoke of a moment ago where POWs were and also where convicts were and persons under investigation. These were sinks, bathrooms, that were the same size upstairs and on the ground floor in both areas, on the ground floor and upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the next page now. Can you tell us what this means, room 36 square metres, what that is all about?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: These are rooms that were in these pavilions and this is the number of square metres of these rooms, 36.9 square metres, then there is a parquet floor in each and every one of them and then in the hallway there was also the office of the guards, or rather, the security who were there. And then there was also a room that was a sort of living room, 64 square metres. So the ground floor and the first floor were the same on both sides and the rooms were practically the same size, and that is where beds were, blankets and mattresses that were used before the war and that is what was used during the war too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In which periods and for how long did you have more than 400 prisoners of war, convicts, prisoners, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: How should I put this? When the KP Dom was established we admitted about 200 prisoners of war; that is to say, in fact the KP Dom on the 1st of August, 1992, had a plan for its security service. In the meantime every day the commission for exchanges was involved in the exchange of these POWs. So in December we received a group on the 15th of December, 1992, 131 POWs who were transferred from Batkovic to us. And from Manjaca when it was disbanded they had been transferred to Batkovic and stayed there for two days. They were brought to us on the 15th of December, 1992, during the night and we were told, since members of the exchange commission accompanied them, we were told that they should spend the night there and that they were supposed to go for an exchange, Tarcin, Celebic. So that group of persons stayed with us for more than a year. The exchange was not carried out, the one that had been agreed upon for the 20th of December, 1992, an all-for-all exchange. The Muslim side did not observe that agreement. Already in the month of February and March, all persons who happened to be at the KP Dom were exchanged except for that group. They had hailed from Grapska these 130. So they were transferred to Rudo to be exchanged for the Serbs from Gorazde and then they were returned to us. So they were exchanged only in 1994. In fact, they were allowed to go to Sarajevo. So in facility D we never had more than 200 POWs and Serbs who were under investigation, about 80, and then there were about 30 convicts as well. If, perchance, the number of persons under investigation would be increased, then we would transfer the convicts to the Igman quarry, that is to say the facilities that had functioned before the war and during the war. As for the other facility in 1994 we had a number of ethnic Croats there. They fled across the Miljacka, they left their weapons behind, and they surrendered to the Serb forces at Grbavica on two occasions. At the end of 1993 about 20 of them fled and about a group of about 50 of them at the end of 1994. They were transferred after being dealt with by the military authorities for two months to our facilities to the other building. They stayed there for about three months until the exchange that was carried out that took them to Kiseljak. I can say quite openly that in one period of time there were three warring armies at the KP Dom at one point in time: Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats, and that there were never any unpleasant situations. On the contrary, they worked together at the farm, within the compound, in the workshop, in the dining hall. Their behaviour was very proper, the behaviour of both, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These Croats, were they exchanged or were they released unilaterally? Who came from Kiseljak? You said that they were exchanged. Did any Serbs come from Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: They were allowed to go to Kiseljak but no Serbs from Kiseljak came.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted, Excellencies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Although it's -- would not be a big problem, can we see the first page and can we zoom in the ICTY stamp. It says -- upper part. Yes. It says this is document consisting of two pages. How come do we have four pages? Do you have any explanation, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Excellency. But it's the Prosecution that prepared this and let us see which pages have ERN numbers and let's try to find our way. Only the first page seems to have an ERN number, none of the others. Perhaps the format is big. Perhaps the page size is different. Perhaps it was A3 or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Do you have any objection, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm trying to assist if I can. I'm just looking at our system, but I have no objection to it being MFI'd. It should be translated, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll mark it for identification pending English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3355, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can. I assume that there was a blueprint and then that is put together in a different way and that is why we have a different page number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at quarter past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the remainder of today we'll be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis with Judge Lattanzi being away due to her official reasons. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to inform the Court that I did look into the document 1D50009, the floor plan document, during the break. It is the -- the document in our system is a two-page document which consists of a cover page and the first page of the exhibit. So the pages 2 through 4 of the exhibit are not from the ICTY document. I don't know where they come from. It doesn't appear to be a problem. They do appear to relate to Kula prison. I just wanted to let the Court know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, on an unrelated note I would just like to note that we have received applications for leave to respond to our motions for subpoenas from General Tolimir, General Miletic, and Hasan Cengic, and we don't oppose any of the leave to responds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Probably, Mr. Karadzic, you may ask the witness who drew that floor plan third or fourth page. Please continue. I'll leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skiljevic, you remember that we leafed through those additional pages. Who drew that floor plan of those rooms?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: The floor plan was drawn by Brckala Nine [phoen] an engineer architect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it faithfully depict the situation there and what is his relationship with your institution?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: It's a fully faithful document and I think that all of that is in accordance with the original plan because he was in charge of the reconstruction of the penitentiary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At some point in your --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, Excellency, would that do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Somewhere in your statement you said that for a while you were in charge of the administration and reception departments of this institution; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how records were kept, in accordance with which regulations, and can you tell us if it is valid and accessible for checks and analysis?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: All the documentation is valid and it was kept in accordance with regulations. If we are talking about the documentation that we had concerning POWs, we received these documents from military organs and others, we registered the persons who came to our institution, we would fill out their record forms, and then they would be released from the KP Dom at some point. Every day records were kept concerning all persons that were the KP Dom, what kind of work they did, where they went. For example, if they went out to work, what kind of work it was; if they were within the compound, what kind of work they did there; if they went for a medical examination, who were the persons that went for a medical examination; if they would stay in hospital for medical treatment, that became part of the records too. So we had complete records for all the persons that were at the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How often would you report to the ministry or someone else about the numbers, about food and so on?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: It is customary for persons who are in such an institution that a duty policeman would bring the numerical level to the, say, head of the kitchen every day and say how many meals were needed for that day. And also if there were some persons who were on special diets, then food would be prepared in accordance with that. So the numerical level had to do with the number of persons who reported to the medical unit too so that the medical officer involved could act in accordance with the situation there if the person involved was supposed to go out for medical treatment or to be administered medication and so on. I, as warden, every day received 24-hour reports on how many persons there were at the KP Dom, where they were, whether there had been any problems in the KP Dom, how many persons went out for medical examinations, how many were kept in hospital, and so on. The duty policeman of the KP Dom was duty-bound to record all of these changes in a document that was called the record for that day and that was the situation throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the barracks, did they take part in feeding their POWs, the one that you were guarding on their behalf?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: We would record the numerical level, that is to say, for example, on a particular day how many persons there were at the KP Dom and we would inform the logistics unit, whatever it was called. They were in charge of food so then we'd send our vehicle out there and then we received that food from the military, say for five months or for --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Five days.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- or a month or something like that. We would prepare the food, cook it in our own kitchens since there were quite a few problems with electricity. Then we would also get big caldrons from them so that we could cook such large amounts of food. That was for POWs and others who received their meals at the KP Dom, so we had no problems whatsoever with regard to food supplies for any persons there and also from the government and the commissioners we received food and even from some of the UN institutions involved.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you start over again. Please put a pause on your part as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have in e-court 1D50010.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That document is one that you referred to in paragraph 35 of your statement so could you please interpret some of these things for us. Can you tell us what this refers to? I see that there's a reference to the barracks. Can you read out the handwritten part so that it could be recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: "Information on the number and feeding of POWs by the army. Certificate certifying that at this moment at the KP Dom Butmir Kula there are 295 persons who are detainees. The transport of food from the barracks of Slobodan Principe Seljo shall be transported by a car of the KP Dom registration number SA 250-963."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: This was just the end of the sight translation. We have not interpreted any of what the witness said afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you repeat what you said after reading out this document, Mr. Skiljevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no, you're not supposed to read it out again, but you said something after reading this.

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: We would give a certificate to the people from our supplies department so that they could take the vehicle to the Slobodan Principe Seljo barracks in order to get food from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this of relevance to us, 02-38 A-B? The handwritten letters and numbers, is that of relevance to us or not? You don't know what this is, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that this sheet of paper was in the possession of the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina and this may be some marking of theirs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3356, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who decided about who would be exchanged and how were you informed about this?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: The commission, the exchange commission, headed by Captain Dragan Bulajic had exclusive authority over that. Bulajic was the head of the commission. The practice was as follows: We would receive a sheet of paper with the names of persons to be exchanged. That sheet bore his signature and we would get it about two hours before the official time of exchange. Upon reception of this list we were duty-bound to give those persons back their belongings if they were deposited and then with their personal effects these persons would get ready and in most times vehicles by the International Red Cross or the UNHCR or even sometimes SFOR vehicles would arrive and those persons would be taken out of the KPD on board those vehicles as agreed by the two exchange commissions. Mostly that's how it went when groups were exchanged. When individuals were exchanged then we would get a list which persons of Serbian ethnicity would be exchanged or possibly somebody would be released without being exchanged. And during that interval of two hours roughly representatives of the ICRC would come and interview the persons in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get 1D50019.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You speak about this document in paragraph 48 of your statement. 1D50019.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I think we received the English translation of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would it be sufficient then to admit it as an associated exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think -- my intention was to admit this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Great. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The names needn't be interpreted so a translation exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, otherwise I would instruct the Registry to admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3358, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, also 1D50027 was a late translation that we were intending to lead live, but if you've also been willing to admit that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber is fine with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we give the number then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3359, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many employees did you have and what were their professional profiles?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: We had about 105 staff in all. At the KPD there were about 70 and the others were on the list of the economy unit. Most of our staff were police officers or guards and there were also educational staff or foremen working with them during the manufacturing process and there were also some staff who worked in the kitchen and other -- did other auxiliary work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us see 1D50014.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please explain if this is the situation on that day, 45 persons under investigation, POWs 88. And what do items 4 and 5 mean, eight persons arrived at the KPD, two persons left. And item 7 reads seven in hospital.

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: This is the report of the duty officer of the KPD on 22 March 1993. On that day 45 persons under investigation were at the KPD, 88 POWs, in all 133. Arrivals eight, departures two. There were no escapes and seven were in hospital. Two Serbs were released from detention and another two were brought in. One Muslim was brought from hospital. Five Muslims were brought from Foca, here the KPD of Foca is meant for the purpose of an exchange scheduled for 23 March 1993, notified warden and guard commander, and there is a signature of the duty officer. This was common practice. We can see from this document that persons were taken to us from other institutions and spent some time at our facility to be exchanged. Since we were close to Sarajevo where most exchanges took place, that is, at the airport and at the Brastvo Jedinstvo bridge. And therefore persons were brought from other penitentiary facilities. They would spend some time waiting because the other side also had to prepare for the exchange. Then the two commissions would compare the lists and once they agreed the exchange took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see the following page. It says this person here, Faruk, stayed longer. He arrived at 1700. How did it happen that this person stayed longer? He is mentioned under item 5. Actually, it's the first remark from above.

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a register of persons at the economy. It shows where they worked on that day, either in the kitchen or the mess room or somewhere else. This person worked at the poultry house where eggs were produced. He arrived at 1700, or rather, 1720 and stayed longer because he was feeding the chickens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So they could stay longer if they wanted to?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was possible. We didn't have any problems with that because we actually didn't guard them. We didn't provide security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It also says in handwriting Ante Grizelj is released and so on. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to the order of the security organ --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please start over from where I broke off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Skiljevic, could you repeat your answer. Please wait a moment before you start giving the answer, please. Could you repeat your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pursuant to the order of the security organ of military post number so and so Grizelj, Ante, was released to reception point Sokolac in order to deal with his status. Ante Grizelj came from Sarajevo and crossed the lines. It follows from this that he was probably being processed by the army and they were trying to resolve his status in contacts with the commission. There were more cases like this, namely, that the security organ who on behalf of the corps was in charge of exchanges to see what they would do with such persons, whether they would be let go to another country, what kind of documents they would get, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that this is a separate document, date is different from the first page, we'll -- the first page was admitted already as an associated exhibit and the second page will be admitted as a separate exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3360, Your Honours, and for the record the first page is Exhibit D3357.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did the hospital treat your detainees? Once their treatment finished did you get any kind of documentation? Did you have information about the state of their health?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Our co-operation with the medical services was excellent. No matter what the category of the persons at the hospital was, we regularly visited and contacted the doctors to learn about the state of their health and we would also receive reports if they had to stay in the hospital longer. We didn't really provide security to these persons at hospital, certainly not when it comes to prisoners of war. We did provide security for Serbs who were under investigation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D50013, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You speak about this document in paragraph 42. Did this apply to civilians in transit too waiting to cross over to the other side?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: It was characteristic that persons who had come to join their families -- I don't know for what reason, but they may have had or they may have lacked medical services from what -- where they had come from. A great percentage of these persons went to Sarajevo and many documents speak to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The exchange or even the release for that exchange did it go smoothly once agreement had been reached or was there stalling and problems?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: There were problems, quite a few. And our institution also had problems with that because when they tell you that a group would arrive and spend the night and eventually they stay for three months. I mentioned a group of 130 persons from Manjaca who were brought to us to be exchanged immediately but that exchange only took place in 1994. So this shows how slowly those exchange commissions worked and somehow they failed to harmonise the exchange lists, the lists of persons. So there were cases when 30 people would be exchanged from the KPD and only three persons were -- arrived from the other side. On the 29th of December, 1992, there was agreement and they -- we insisted that it be an all-for-all exchange. 210 for 205 persons who were at the Butmir KPD or other facilities at the RS, they were to be exchanged for persons held by the BH army but the exchange didn't take place because the two sides were unable to harmonise the lists. The Muslim side was unwilling to release Serbs taken prisoners from their own camps for the persons in our detention because they considered them persons from other areas. So these persons remained at the KPD for over a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who insisted on the all-for-all principle? You were mentioned, us and them, but who was it who actually insisted?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Our side assisted on the all for all principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned me?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: You were informed by Mr. Dragan Bulajic, the commission president. Before that 30 persons from the KPD had been exchanged for only four Serbian KPD from the silos. And this was considered to be a ruse. Mr. Bulajic informed you and you insisted that an all-for-all exchange be made. When Manjaca was closed down, the people came to us by way of Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3361, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now the last document. Can you please tell us how the jobs were assigned and was there a difference between the work done by Serbian detainees on the one hand and Muslim and Croatian detainees on the other?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as the work and occupational therapy go at the KPD, there were labour units with the Ekonomija where convicts were sent and people under investigation and where also Muslim and Croatian POWs worked. There was no discrimination and there are documents to show that. They also worked in the kitchen together and in the workshops and in the chicken farm. Serbs, Croats, and Muslims worked together. I said earlier that no situation of conflict was recorded. I was never informed of any problem between these persons. They worked together and shared the same faith.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see 1D50021.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And tell us what this is on page 1. 1D50021. We can remove the previous document and zoom in on this -- oh, I see that there is a translation. Can you tell us what this is about. It says work site, kitchen, and so on. Are these the places where they worked?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a daily register of the persons working at the individual work sites. Some people went to the kitchen, some to the boiler room or the warehouse, the library, car repair shop, and then a list of persons going to a work site is made and the hour of their departure and the hour of their return is recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We see at the library there was Srebrov and there were others, but we can see that there were Serbian, Croatian, and Muslim names; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can see the name of Zukic under dining hall. What is this person's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Huso Zukic, he's a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Next page, please. Oh, I'm sorry, we see prisoners of war at the top of the page and this is the page for the convicts; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's a handwritten heading; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3362, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies. I have no more questions for Mr. Skiljevic at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson and Mr. Karadzic, having heard kind explanation of Ms. Gustafson, the Chamber is of the view that the 1D50029 which was referred to in para 57 can be admitted as an associated exhibit. Shall we give the number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3363, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And 27, if I understood properly, has also been admitted; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. What we didn't admit is 25 and 26. Very well. Mr. Skiljevic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in most part in writing, that is, through your written statement in lieu of your oral testimony. And now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Mr. Skiljevic.

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I just want to clarify a point you made in your statement. As I understand it from paragraphs 4 and 5 of your statement between the 6th of April, 1992, and the 18th of May when you returned to Kula to work on the farm, you were never at the Kula prison compound although you went to the prison farm a few times. Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And it's also clear from paragraph 5 that from the 18th of May until the 1st of August, 1992, when Kula began to function under the Ministry of Justice your position is that your movement was restricted. You worked on the farm, you slept on the farm, you could not enter the administration buildings or other facilities. And since you always stayed and slept at the farm you do not know what went on within the prison compound during this period of time. I'm going to put it to you that those assertions are untrue, that in fact you were inside the Kula prison compound at least twice after the 6th of April, 1992, and before the 18th of May, where you met with police and Kula prison officials. That from the 18th of May when you began working at the farm you didn't sleep at the farm but you in fact slept at the medical building of the prison. And you actually have substantial information about what was happening in the prison compound prior to the time that the Ministry of Justice took over its operations in August, including knowledge that Mico Stanisic, Momcilo Mandic, and Tomo Kovac visited Kula during this time. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, that question is so complex and compound I think it's impossible for the witness to answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Could you break down?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sure. Why don't we go to 65 ter 24324 and we can start at page 77 of that document and I'll break it down.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, you recall, Mr. Skiljevic, being interviewed by the Office of the Prosecution of this Tribunal in December 2003 at the premises of the Kula prison; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is a transcript of that audio-recorded interview. It's only in English so I will read the relevant parts to you. The question in the middle of page 77 is: "And after that, did you come back to Kula ... in the course of April 1992?" "A. In April 1992, during the course of April 1992, I came here a couple of times. This facility had already been taken, for about 50 per cent of it was taken. My office was broken into. A police member Supic Branko was in it. He worked at the airport before and we came from the same village. The duty officer of Dom, so to say, of the ex-Dom, were unknown persons to me, except for the chief Mladen Krstojevic, who was in the kitchen. When I came here on the 20th of April, I found police commander Vujicic Radenko, who informed me that they had sent a car to pick up the prison warden, the Dom warden, and if there's time ... I waited and at 13.30 Lalovic Ratko came." And then the question was: "Just one more question: You say it was on the 20th of April. Is that correct? "A. Yes." And if we could go to the next page of this interview.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask -- may you pose a question, please, because otherwise we will be getting a very compound question again.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It will not be a compound question. I'm just covering the statements where the witness talked about his presence in April 1992 and there is one more perhaps two more short extracts.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: "And how come you remember perfectly that it was on the 20th of April, 1992? Was there anything specific on that day that makes you remember that day perfectly?" Was the question. And your answer is: "I just know. I remember everything perfectly. 21st of April at 8.00 a meeting was held with 20 employees of KP Dom ..." And at the bottom of page 79, you're asked: "Where did the meeting take place on the 21st?" And at the top of page 80 you say: "On the ground floor of this building in a room." And you're asked: "And has that building got a name?" And you answer: "Admin building." Mr. Skiljevic, contrary to what you stated today, you were clearly present at the Kula prison compound at least twice during April 1992, on the 20th and the 21st; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 90 of this document, you're asked: "So you remain in the premises of KP Dom Kula as of the 18th of May, 1992, until when?" And you answer: "I stayed from the 18th of May until the 2nd of December, 2003." And you're asked: "If I understood correctly you would be living in KP Dom Kula?" And you answered: "I was living in KP Dom Kula, in the premises of the medical centre until the end of August 1992, and from then I was living in an apartment of the republic inspector Kemo Alisahovic until 2.5 years ago. The apartment is 30 metres away from KP Dom." So again, Mr. Skiljevic, in 2003 you were unequivocal when you told the OTP that you were living in the prison's medical centre from the 18th of May until the end of August, not at the prison farm as you now claim; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: The premises of the prison farm are at a distance of around 100 metres. There is a building which was also called the health centre. It is true that there is another health centre in the administration building. We slept at the health centre at the Ekonomija, that is to say the farm. It is also correct that I came there on the 6th of April, that on the 7th of April I came and got the car, and that I came to ask what was to be done because at the order of the warden Mr. Kreho Fadil, the entire security service left to work at the central prison in Sarajevo. And the remaining personnel I was chief of the correctional service were left in the lurch. We didn't --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. My question was simply about where you were living and you've answered that. I don't need these additional details right now. Now if we could go to page 97 of this document you were asked: "We were discussing the fact that you remember having seen Mr. Mico Stanisic come to KP Dom Kula. Do you remember if it was at the time when the SJB Kula under the control of Milenko Tepavcevic was in charge of the premises?" Your answer: "Yes." And a few lines down: "You physically saw him in the premises? "A. Yes, he was in the office. "Q. In which office? "A. With Tepavcevic. "Q. You mentioned that you didn't know him from before and you were not introduced to him, so how come you can be certain that it was Mr. Mico Stanisic being with Tepavcevic?" And you answered: "Continuously being here I saw and learnt from talking to other employees who would come and who was present there." And on the next page you're asked: "Such as, for instance? "A. Kovac Tomo, Minister Mandic, his deputy." You were asked: "What was his name? "A. Nenad Radovic ..." And then you refer to meeting a number of judges. And at page 108 you said: "So after you come back on the 18th of May, 1992, you mentioned that you had contact with minister of justice and his deputy Radovic. Did they have an office here in KP Dom Kula? "A. Minister Mandic had one." And at page 109 you say -- you were asked: "In which building?" And you answer: "In the admin building." And you're asked: "And do you know since when he had an office in the admin building?" And you say: "I think since mid-June, I'm not sure about the date." Now, at paragraph 5 of your witness statement you said that you did not know what went on within the KP Dom compound between the 18th of May and August of 1992, but as these passages I read out to you indicate you have substantial information about what was happening at the prison compound during that time; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You don't deny that all this information about Mr. Mandic visiting, Mr. Stanisic visiting, Mr. Mandic having an office in Kula prison, Mr. Kovac visiting Kula, that information was all correct that I read out to you, right, that's information you learned at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please be given more specific dates or times and Kula is also a big location. Whether it was the prison compound or the ministry or the public security station because they're all different. It's as if someone said Scheveningen and Scheveningen is an entire suburb.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, that's ridiculous. This was a prison and in any event the passages I read out were clear as to the time and indeed the locations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, excuse me, I would ask Ms. Gustafson to ask whether the public security station was a part of the prison, whether the ministry was part of the prison, whether the administration building was located within the compound because it's all confused. On page 85 he says, or rather, page 95 of the interview he says he doesn't know when he saw Stanisic. He doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: These are all questions Dr. Karadzic can raise in re-direct. I'm putting this witness's own words to him and asking him to confirm that they're accurate. I think that's completely fair in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Skiljevic, the passages I read out to you about Mr. Stanisic's presence, Mr. Kovac's presence, Mr. Mandic's presence, Mr. Mandic's having an office in Kula as of mid-June in the administration building, that's all correct information, information that you had at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Mandic was the justice minister, and at the time the expert teams worked together because as early as on the 16th of June Mr. President signed that penal and correctional institutions were to be formed and courts. So it wasn't only Kula. It was about applying the regulations, the daily schedules, and so on, that is to say establishing law and order so that the KP Dom would begin to operate. And another thing, the labour unit Privrednik never stopped because some of us in fact worked in this economic or labour unit. It's true that he had a temporary office in the administration building, but we didn't have any other offices because the police station Kula was located there. They took over these offices up until the 1st of August, 1992, when they moved into another building which was within the KP Dom. And the other facilities that you mentioned that I said in my statement we couldn't reach, it's true that we couldn't reach these facilities. They are registered as facility D2, where persons were accommodated and it's about 70 metres away. And within the Kula compound itself, there are seven buildings. And as Ekonomija we had four buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I would tender the last four pages I put to the witness, pages 97 to 98 and 108 and 109.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D6277, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Skiljevic, I'm going to ask you to focus very carefully on the specific questions that I ask and I will try to keep my questions specific as much as possible. Now, you mentioned in your testimony earlier today at page 64 that investigators from this Tribunal went to the Kula prison in 2003 and photocopied a number of documents. Now, you were still the Kula prison warden at that time and you, in fact, assisted the investigators in accessing the documents that they copied; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: I received a notice, in fact, or an order from the Ministry of Justice that it was my duty as the warden to hand over all the documents and show them for inspection. And as far as I know, these were investigators from ICTY who came there and of course we gave them all the documents for inspection without any problems. They copied something, they took away something else. And after a while they would return the documents because there were quite a lot of documents and that is all correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: We will be looking at a number of those documents the investigators copied and for the information of the Court and the Defence the ERN ranges of those documents are 0297-6517 through to 0297-8661. Now, if we could go to 65 ter 1D50004, which I presume has an exhibit number at this point.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3343, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Skiljevic, this is one of the documents that is discussed at paragraph 28 of your statement and as I understand it this is a document that you, in fact, provided to the Defence. Is that correct; and if so, where did you get this document, please?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: I received this document from the president of the commission for exchange, Mr. Bulajic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to hand to you as well as to the Court and the Defence a hard copy of this document which is attached to a copy of Exhibit P1127, which is the identical document with some slight difference in terms of the handwritten markings that are on it. If I could ask for the assistance of the usher, please. Now, Mr. Skiljevic, you can see that the first document, the one that's also on our screen, has some handwritten markings on it, in particular the words 10.000 referring to the number of Muslim civilians who had passed through Kula at that point - this is near the end of the first paragraph - has been crossed out and the words "exactly 119 civilians" has been written in by hand. And there's also some highlighting and underlining on this document that are not on the ICTY exhibit. So I'd like to ask you who made these markings to this document, if you know?
