utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: This document was used before the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a piece of evidence provided by me. Witness Dragan Bulajic who testified wrote an incorrect piece of information here, that there were 10.000 people and he then refuted that before the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He said that he signed it without looking because I was the one who intervened by saying that this piece of information was not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So was it you who crossed out the words "ten thousand" and added in the words "exactly 119 civilians" to this document?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly if it was him or me, but there was a dispute about this and I then intervened in court and I said that there were around 119 or 120 civilians. That was the exact number of the civilians who had come there, and he agreed with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you say you don't know exactly if it was him or me. You're saying it may have been you who crossed out the words "ten thousand" and added the words "exactly 119 civilians" or it may have been Mr. Bulajic. When was this change made to the document? Was this something that was done in preparation for your trial at the state court in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So you can confirm that the -- and, in fact, the second document in this -- in these two documents I handed to you, as I said, is the same document without these handwritten markings and it is one of the documents that the OTP copied at Kula prison in 2003. Also based on that and your evidence just now it's clear that at the time this document was received at Kula prison, it did not have these handwritten markings. That was something that was done much later; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, at paragraphs 13 and 36 of your statement you refer to Dr. Karadzic's visit to Kula prison in August of 1992, and you've discussed that as well in your testimony earlier today. And you said earlier today that Mr. Mandic told you that a high-level delegation would be coming to the prison just an hour or an hour and a half before the delegation, in fact, arrived. And you said that Mr. Mandic did not tell you that Dr. Karadzic would be in that delegation, and that was at page 56. That's not true, Mr. Skiljevic. In fact, Mr. Mandic told you two to three days in advance that a delegation headed by Dr. Karadzic would be coming to Kula prison; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic also told you that a lot of journalists would be coming with the delegation, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And Mr. Mandic also instructed you to prepare decisions to release some prisons for Mr. Karadzic to hand out during that visit and you did that; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to page 173 of 65 ter 24324. This is again from the interview you gave to the Prosecution in 2003. And you state: "I was informed by the minister of justice, Mr. Mandic, that a delegation would be coming headed by the President of the Republic and the members of the international community and a great number of journalists would come to visit this Dom. Well, the exact date, I think it was the beginning of August, in the period of time between 1500 hours and 1600 hours. He told me to prepare a number of decisions, that a number is to be released on parole, and that it would be suitable, appropriate, that those decisions are handed over to them by Mr. President." And you're asked: "Did you prepare these release orders or release certificates?" And you answered: "Yes." And then at page 175 you're asked: "I would like to come back to the visit of Mr. Karadzic." You mentioned that you were informed by Momcilo Mandic that there would be that visit. "A. Yes. "Q. How many days before or how many weeks before? "A. I think two or three days, not more." Mr. Skiljevic, as you told the OTP in 2003, Mr. Mandic told you about this visit two or three days before it happened. He told you that Mr. Karadzic himself would be there and he told you that there would be a large number of journalists present; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: It is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Mr. Mandic told you to prepare decisions for release of prisoners which you did, and in the video of this visit which is P2840, we can see Dr. Karadzic handing those decisions out. You would have had to have known about this visit at least a day or two in advance in order to select prisoners and prepare their release decisions; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Mandic didn't tell me. It was another person who told me, but this other person did not say that Dr. Karadzic would come. In that interval, I wasn't even the warden.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And Mr. Mandic told you in preparing these decisions to release prisoners to select prisoners who were elderly and in poor health, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, during this visit Dr. Karadzic was interviewed and he told CNN: "We released only people who are not likely to be mobilised again." Now, I take it that you when you were preparing these release decisions had no idea whether or not the elderly and sick prisoners whom you selected for release had ever been mobilised by the other side; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I would like to tender pages 173 and 175 of this interview, either as a separate number or as part of the P6277, whichever the Court prefers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll add them to P6277.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Skiljevic, at paragraph 6 of your statement you said: "I did not know the legal grounds for the detention of these people as this was exclusively within the jurisdiction of the military. They decided who was going to be assigned where and they decided their status." And at paragraph 7 you said that when you took over the KP Dom prisoners from the jurisdiction of the police "we were told that they were prisoners of war and that the prisoners of war were under the authority of the military." Now, these people you refer to as prisoners of war they were for the most part brought to Kula prison by the army; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And although you made it clear in your statement you weren't involved in determining the status of these prisoners, you do know that they were overwhelming of Muslim and Croat ethnicity; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And although they were labelled prisoners of war, you also knew that many of these people were not prisoners of war, they were simply people who lived in Serb-held territory and belonged to the other ethnic groups; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, let's look at what you said in 2003 about this. If we could go to page 146 of this document that is still on the screen. And you're asked: "You've been working in the prison system for quite many years. Could you give me a definition as to what is a prisoner of war?" And you answer: "You mean the Geneva Convention?" And you're asked: "I mean what is your knowledge of the definition of the prisoner of war and at the time what that meant to you?" And you answer: "Theory and practice are two different things. My logic tells me bringing people from one area of another ethnic group is not a prisoner of war." And you're asked: "So that's what was happening in practice?" And you answer: "Correct." And then you're asked: "So all civilians from specific areas who were non-Serbs would be arrested?" And you answer: "Unless they fled. Or if they had not gone to front lines. Or another example, during combat activities they surrender to one or the other side. There were such cases as well. Third, 70 Croats are fleeing over Miljacka river from Sarajevo to Serb territory. And after the military processing, they come to prison here and they leave here, live and sound, to be exchanged or without the exchange. The fourth issue, from KP Dom Srbinje, Foca, they come here, stay here for a while, and the exchange takes place. And at the end from all the prisons they come here, and central exchange is taking place. Dayton is completed, and end the war. No prisoners of war. Question mark." Now, in 2003 when you spoke to the OTP you agreed that what was happening in practice was that non-Serb civilians, people who you did not consider to be prisoners of war, were being arrested and detained; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Civilians were not arrested or detained. Rather, they were brought to the KP Dom for family reunification, if you are referring to the area of the municipality of Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, we'll look at some of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now I'd like to tender this page as well as part of P6277.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be also added.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to 65 ter 1D50018, which again has an exhibit number but I'm not aware of what that is at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3350, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could go to page 10 of the English and page 6 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Skiljevic, you stated at paragraph 47 that these documents and one of which is on the screen now showed that Kula helped in humanitarian cases and facilitated civilians crossing and family reunion. So I take it that all the people listed in this document and the others that come together with it were civilians; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, the people on this particular document with the surname Zahiragic, we can see there's six females and four males, some of them are quite young and one woman in particular is quite elderly, where were they -- these people with the surname Zahiragic from?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: From Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. The subject of this -- do you know, were they all related to each other? Do you know that? They all have the same surname.

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Omer Zahiragic is the husband of Meira Zahiragic. Their daughter is Serveta Zahiragic, I think, because she was a prosecution witness before the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that's how come I know, because these people are my age.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And the subject of this letter is reuniting families. Can you tell us what were the specific details of the family reunification that was going on here? Who was being reunified with whom?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: I did not study this subject matter, you see, because -- well, from experience I know that as far as family reunification is concerned some families left earlier on, perhaps at the beginning of the war, whereas these families lived in Serb territory throughout the war and they expressed the wish to go to Sarajevo. That was done by the exchanges commission, UNPROFOR, UNHCR, liaison officers, without us being involved. We were just there to provide good services if they were supposed to stay with us or spend the night there until they went to Sarajevo. That was our help, if you will, to these families in some way.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So what you're saying is you actually don't know specifically what's going on here, who is being reunited with who. With respect to this particular family you don't know those details; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: I know that the family went to Sarajevo. This document shows it all.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to the next page, please, which is another similar document referring to mostly people from the Planja family and two people from the Zahiragic family. Now, these people with the surname of Planja, where were they from, were they also from Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this letter is dated the 24th of January, 1995. How long have they been kept at Kula?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: From five days to two months. I cannot be more precise. You can tell by these dates. One group left and then the paperwork had been done, and after that the second group would leave and so on. And they all really left.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, one of your own documents that, in fact, Dr. Karadzic showed you earlier, D3362, work site lists, indicate that Rasema Planja and Azra Planja and Amela Planja, the first three names on this list were all working on the farm on the 26th of November, 1994. So at least these three prisoners would have been in Kula for at least two months; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: I said that I didn't know the exact duration. It could be between five days and three months. So depending on when an individual was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And these civilian prisoners were also put to work like the other prisoners; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: It is characteristic of civilians that since these people were farmers in Rogatica municipality they didn't want to stay indoors and they wanted to go out and work so as not to be bored. So they milked cows and what have you and worked together with the convicts that had been brought from Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to the next page of this document which lists five individuals with the surname of Katica. The Chamber has received evidence that some people with this surname were transferred from Vrbarija village in Sokolac, but a village near Rogatica to Kula. Were these people with the surname Katica from Vrbarija?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: They must have been from the area of Rogatica, Sokolac, thereabouts. But to ask me about the specific village ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the Chamber has received evidence a Sokolac SJB document stating that 61 civilians from Vrbarija were transferred to Kula on the 29th of October, 1994, and has received evidence that people with the name Katica were among them, and that's D3189 and P6235. So would you agree that these individuals from Vrbarija were -- sorry, this document is dated the 23rd of January, 1995. These individuals had been held at Kula for almost three months; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm about to move on to another relatively lengthy document so if Your Honours would permit me to break at this moment. I would also like to provide the witness with hard copies of 65 ter 24211 and 24236. These are Kula prison records that are somewhat lengthy and I would like to give the witness a fair opportunity to look at them and review them. And if he would be so kind as to do that out of court this afternoon I would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, that sounds like a very good idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Skiljevic, we'll be -- I'll be asking you about these documents most likely tomorrow, although the schedule's a little up in the air. So if you could be so kind as to review them and familiarise yourself with them, I think you may find that they are familiar to you, I would appreciate that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC
utterances.text: Does a question follow now?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, Mr. Skiljevic. I should have been more clear. It's time for the court to break today so I will be asking you about these documents and other documents when we reconvene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gustafson. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. At the outset of this session Mr. Robinson noted that the Defence has no objection to the request for leave to respond concerning the subpoenas. That's the Tolimir, Miletic, and Cengic subpoenas. I just wanted to note that the Prosecution also has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then the Chamber will hereby issue the oral ruling. The Chamber grants the request by Hasan Cengic filed today to respond to the accused's motion to subpoena Hasan Cengic filed on the 21st of March, 2013. The Chamber further grants the request by Radivoje Miletic also filed today to respond to the accused's motion to subpoena Radivoje Miletic filed on the 2nd of April, 2013. And I'll also request the Registry to communicate these oral rulings to the relevant witnesses. Mr. Skiljevic, we'll adjourn for today and continue tomorrow sometime in the morning or in the afternoon, after the next witness's evidence is over. I'd like to advise you, Mr. Skiljevic, not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony while you are staying here at The Hague while you are giving evidence. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 9th day of April, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.47 p.m.,
